Underscore_ est un talk-show tech lancé: Underscore_ is a tech talk show launched in 2021 by Micode — Michaël de Marliave — with Matthieu Lambda and Tiffany Souterre, Developer Advocate at Amazon Web Services. It started live on Twitch on Wednesday evenings, before being re-edited for YouTube and then released as a podcast. The name itself is a developer joke: the underscore, the low dash you slip between two words in a variable name.
Le parcours de son fondateur explique be: Its founder's background explains a lot about the show's tone. No elite school: a two-year IT diploma, and a first video — "I hacked scammers on Leboncoin" — that won him tens of thousands of subscribers in twenty-four hours. He taught himself cybersecurity, openly inspired by science popularisers. He took their method and applied it to a more worrying question: how you get hacked.
Quand un invité part sur la vectorisatio: When a guest launches into vectorising embeddings, Micode brings them back with a simple question, unashamed. It's his greatest quality: in front of the screen, there's someone who doesn't know either.
Jamy de C'est pas sorcier, des experts e: Jamy from C'est pas sorcier, cyber experts working for governments, published researchers. People you'd pay 200 euros a seat to hear at a conference. Here it's free — and that's never trumpeted.
Un chercheur, une journaliste spécialisé: A researcher, a specialist journalist and an entrepreneur around a table. After an hour and a half, you've understood something true — not a lightly dressed-up Wikipedia summary.
Une référence du podcast tech francophon: A reference of French-language tech podcasting, and the word isn't overused: Underscore_ has built something rare, a long show on a niche subject that reaches widely without betraying its geek soul. The production follows — set, lighting, sound — and the channel now exceeds 950,000 subscribers on YouTube.
Le vrai reproche est ailleurs, et il tie: The real criticism lies elsewhere, and it fits in one word: the replay. The show is a live Twitch stream, which becomes a replay, re-edited into a shorter version for YouTube, from which the audio is extracted for the podcast. Four layers. Depending on the platform, the length changes and you don't get the same show — the live runs ninety minutes, YouTube serves sixty, the podcast sometimes less. For the loyal listener, it creates an odd feeling: that of having already seen what they're watching, because they literally have. It's a rich person's problem — that of someone producing too many good things not to end up rebroadcasting them.
